### Thailand Agriculture Export Data


## Library 

```{r}

library(ggplot2)
library(ggfortify)
library(fpp2)
library(forecast)
library(TSstudio)
library(urca)
library(tseries)

```

## Data


```{r}

data <- read.csv('AgriData.csv')

export_data <- ts(data$Export,frequency = 12,start = c(2013,1))

export_data

```


## Time Series Decomposition


```{r}

autoplot(export_data) + labs(title = "Thai agricultural export value", y = "Million baht", x = NULL)

ggseasonplot(export_data,continuous = TRUE,polar = TRUE)

ggsubseriesplot(export_data)

ts_seasonal(export_data,type = "all")


```
## White noise?

From Ljung-Box we can see that the data isn't white-noise so it has something to forecast.

```{r}


Box.test(export_data, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box")


```


## Stationarity (For ARIMA model)

After one diff you can see that the time series is stationary so we can show that optimal params for ARIMA is d=1 and D=0

```{r}

#Unit Root Test

export_data %>% diff() %>% ur.kpss() %>% summary() #KPSS

export_data %>% diff() %>% adf.test() #ADF

export_data %>% diff() %>% ggtsdisplay()

nsdiffs(export_data)

BoxCox.lambda(export_data)

```
## Train Test Split 

We use data from **2013- 9/2022** to forecast to avoid unexpected growth in trend.

```{r}

n <- length(export_data)              
n_train <- floor(0.8 * n)             

train <- window(export_data, end = c(2022, 9))
test  <- window(export_data, start = c(2022, 10))
h <- length(test)                     

length(train); length(test)                           

```

## Model Selection

In this step we set Naive Forecasting Method to the baseline.


```{r}

fc_naive  <- naive(train, h = h)
fc_snaive <- snaive(train, h = h)

# ETS 
fit_ets <- ets(train)
fc_ets  <- forecast(fit_ets, h = h)

# Holt-Winters, additive and multiplicative seasonality
fc_hw_add  <- hw(train, h = h, seasonal = "additive")
fc_hw_mult <- hw(train, h = h, seasonal = "multiplicative")

# ARIMA and SARIMA,
fit_arima  <- auto.arima(train, seasonal = FALSE, stepwise = FALSE, approximation = FALSE)
fit_sarima <- auto.arima(train, seasonal = TRUE,  stepwise = FALSE, approximation = FALSE)
fc_arima   <- forecast(fit_arima,  h = h)
fc_sarima  <- forecast(fit_sarima, h = h)

```



# Residual Checks

Since SARIMA is the only model that error is white-noise so we will use it for point and interval forecast.

```{r}
lb <- function(res, fitdf = 0) {
  r <- Box.test(na.omit(res), lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = fitdf)
  c(Q = unname(r$statistic), p = r$p.value)
}

resids <- list(
  Naive   = residuals(fc_naive),
  SNaive  = residuals(fc_snaive),
  ETS     = residuals(fit_ets),
  HW_add  = residuals(fc_hw_add),
  HW_mult = residuals(fc_hw_mult),
  ARIMA   = residuals(fit_arima),
  SARIMA  = residuals(fit_sarima)
)
fitdf <- c(Naive = 0, SNaive = 0, ETS = 0, HW_add = 0, HW_mult = 0,
           ARIMA = length(coef(fit_arima)), SARIMA = length(coef(fit_sarima)))

round(t(mapply(lb, resids, fitdf)), 4)

checkresiduals(fit_ets, lag = 24)
checkresiduals(fit_arima,lag = 24)
checkresiduals(fit_sarima, lag = 24)
```

## Model Comparison

```{r}
metrics <- function(pred, actual, train) {
  e <- as.numeric(actual) - as.numeric(pred)
  c(RMSE = sqrt(mean(e^2)),
    MAE  = mean(abs(e)),
    MAPE = mean(abs(e / as.numeric(actual))) * 100)
}

preds <- list(Naive = fc_naive$mean, SNaive = fc_snaive$mean,
              ETS = fc_ets$mean, HW_add = fc_hw_add$mean, HW_mult = fc_hw_mult$mean,
              ARIMA = fc_arima$mean, SARIMA = fc_sarima$mean)

res <- t(sapply(preds, metrics, actual = test, train = train))
round(res[order(res[, "RMSE"]), ], 2)

autoplot(window(export_data, start = 2020))+
  autolayer(fc_snaive$mean,series = "SNaive")+
  autolayer(fc_ets$mean,series = "ETS")+
  autolayer(fc_hw_add$mean,series = "HW additive")+
  autolayer(fc_sarima$mean,series = "SARIMA")+
  autolayer(test,series = "Actual")

```
## Point and Interval Forecast

```{r}
# Check that the intervals behave on the holdout
fc <- forecast(fit_sarima, h = h, level = c(80, 95))
mean(test >= fc$lower[, 2] & test <= fc$upper[, 2])   
mean(test >= fc$lower[, 1] & test <= fc$upper[, 1])   

# Final model on all data, and the 12-month forecast
fit_final <- auto.arima(export_data, stepwise = FALSE, approximation = FALSE)
checkresiduals(fit_final, lag = 24)
fc_final <- forecast(fit_final, h = 12, level = c(80, 95))
fc_final
autoplot(fc_final)
```
## Conclusion

Thai agricultural export value is a non-stationary, seasonal series that needs one difference (d = 1) and no variance transformation. Of the seven models compared, **SARIMA(0,1,4)(1,0,0)[12]** is the final choice because it’s the only one with valid residuals, so it’s the only one whose prediction intervals you can defend.

what we find in this project:

1.ETS was best (RMSE 10,277, MAPE 5.88%), followed closely by Holt-Winters additive (10,500). Naive scored 13,648, and SARIMA scored 19,050, worse than both Naive and ETS.

2.Residual diagnostics: only SARIMA passed the Ljung-Box test (p = 0.49). ETS and Holt-Winters failed because they miss the lag-4 and lag-12 dependence.

3.Final model: SARIMA, chosen for statistical validity, with the forecast and its 80% and 95% intervals taken from that one model.
